analysis.one_liner: Caps jury awards for pain and suffering, shields FDA-approved drug makers from punitive damages, and restricts lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill never reached a Senate vote — its sponsor chaired the committee that held one hearing on it in July 1995, and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten personal-injury law nationwide. It would have capped punitive damages at three times actual losses or $250,000, required injured people to prove outrageous conduct by a heightened standard, and barred repeat punitive awards against a company for the same conduct. It would have capped pain-and-suffering awards in medical malpractice cases at $250,000, given drug and device makers near-immunity from punitive damages once the FDA approved their product, ended shared liability for pain-and-suffering awards, made it easier to dismiss and charge fees to prisoners who sue, and shifted legal fees onto plaintiffs who reject a settlement offer and then win less at trial.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporate defendants and their insurers gain the most: predictable, capped exposure in lawsuits brought by injured people. Drug and medical device makers gain a shield from punitive damages whenever the FDA approved the product, unless they defrauded the agency. Physicians, hospitals, and health plans gain the $250,000 malpractice cap and a shorter two-year window to sue, which lowers malpractice insurance costs. Prison systems gain tighter rules for dismissing inmate lawsuits. The bill also targets plaintiffs' trial lawyers with fee disclosure requirements and mandatory sanctions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drug makers, insurers, hospitals, corporate defendants

how_it_helps.text: Caps punitive damages nationwide: claimants must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant intended harm or acted with conscious, flagrant disregard, and awards are limited to three times economic damages or $250,000, whichever is greater.

Bars punitive damages against drug and medical device manufacturers whenever the FDA approved the product or it met FDA safety rules — unless the company withheld or misrepresented material information to the FDA or bribed an agency official.

Caps pain-and-suffering awards in health care liability actions at $250,000 no matter how many defendants or claims, sets a two-year deadline to sue, and lets defendants pay future damages in installments that stop if the injured person dies or returns to work.
Ends joint liability for noneconomic damages, so each defendant pays only its own percentage of a pain-and-suffering award even if others responsible for the injury cannot pay their share.

Prohibits punitive damages against a defendant for conduct that has already been the basis of punitive damages elsewhere, with an exception only for newly discovered, substantial evidence of additional wrongdoing.

Requires prisoners who sue without paying fees to disclose all assets and pay filing fees according to ability to pay, makes it mandatory for courts to dismiss claims that fail to state a claim or allege only insubstantial injury, and blocks prisoner civil rights suits until prison grievance systems are exhausted.

Tightens rules on expert witnesses (requiring generally accepted, tested methods and disqualifying witnesses paid contingent on the outcome), makes Rule 11 sanctions for abusive filings mandatory, and requires plaintiffs who reject a settlement offer and then win no more at trial to pay the defendant's costs and attorney fees.

analysis.who_pays: Injured people bear the cost. Medical malpractice victims — including the catastrophically injured — would be limited to $250,000 for pain and suffering no matter how severe the harm. People hurt by FDA-approved drugs or devices would largely lose punitive damages, the main legal tool for punishing companies that put dangerous products on the market. People injured by several parties would absorb the unpaid share of any defendant who is insolvent or unknown. Plaintiffs who turn down settlement offers would risk paying the defense's legal fees. Prisoners would face new fees and dismissal rules for civil rights claims.

drawbacks.text: A $250,000 cap on pain-and-suffering damages applies regardless of how catastrophic the injury — a child with lifelong brain damage from a delivery error would recover the same noneconomic amount as someone with a minor injury — and juries would not be told the cap exists while their awards are cut afterward.

The FDA-approval shield would bar punitive damages even when a drug or device later harms people in ways the FDA review missed; only outright fraud on the agency reopens the door, meaning the FDA's judgment, not a jury's, would largely decide accountability.

Ending joint liability for noneconomic damages means an injured person eats the loss whenever one responsible party is bankrupt, uninsured, or never identified — the bill requires juries to assign shares even to people who are not parties to the case.

The settlement-fee rule would pressure injured plaintiffs with limited funds to accept early offers, since rejecting an offer and winning no more at trial makes them liable for the defendant's costs and attorney fees, and the fee is capped at local hourly rates.

The prisoner provisions would require dismissal of suits alleging only 'insubstantial' injury and block civil rights claims until administrative remedies are exhausted, which can swallow legitimate claims about unsafe or abusive conditions.

The bill's stated defense — that limits would lower insurance costs and deter frivolous suits — rests on the claim that savings would reach consumers through lower prices and premiums, an indirect benefit the bill does not guarantee anywhere in its text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's strongest defensible pieces are the one-punitive-award rule for mass torts (so a company is not punished dozens of times for the same act) and the stricter expert-witness standards, which screen out junk science on both sides. But the core of the bill transfers risk from insurers and manufacturers onto the people least able to bear it: the hardest-hit malpractice victims and people injured by approved drugs face fixed, low ceilings, while the industry benefits are immediate and certain. The cost-shifting and fee-disclosure provisions aimed at trial lawyers would also raise the price of suing for people who can only afford a contingency fee. On balance, the costs to injured people outweigh the stated efficiency gains.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee — chaired by its own sponsor — through a single hearing in July 1995, and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997 without ever coming to a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Orrin Hatch, chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, introduced the bill on April 4, 1995 with two Republican cosponsors, Mitch McConnell and Craig Thomas.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Judiciary Committee, which Hatch himself chaired.
The committee held a hearing on July 26, 1995, but never voted the bill out of committee, and the full Senate never debated it.
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill expired with it — no roll call was ever taken on it in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured people came out ahead in the narrow sense that the existing legal system — uncapped pain-and-suffering awards, no FDA-approval shield, shared liability — remained in place. The corporate defendants, drug makers, and insurers that wanted the caps gained nothing from this bill, though similar proposals kept coming back in later Congresses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured people; existing tort law unchanged

for.name: Orrin Hatch
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-UT), Chairman, Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the committee he chaired and held a hearing on it in July 1995; never brought it to a markup or floor vote.

for.name: Tort reform and insurance industry coalitions
for.role: Business, insurance, and health industry groups
for.what_they_did: Pressed Congress throughout the mid-1990s for national limits on punitive damages, product liability, and malpractice awards.

against.name: Plaintiffs' trial lawyer bar
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the mid-1990s tort reform agenda, arguing damage caps would bar the courtroom door for the most seriously injured.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party breakdown exists; all three sponsors were Republicans, and the tort reform fights of that era generally split along party lines.

industries.industry: Prescription drug and medical device makers
industries.note: The bill bars punitive damages against any FDA-approved drug or device — the main punishment tool for putting dangerous products on the market — unless the company defrauded the agency. The malpractice title also sweeps in 'the manufacturer, distributor, supplier, marketer, promoter, or seller of a medical product' and caps pain-and-suffering awards against them at $250,000.

A hard $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages, a two-year filing deadline, installment payments that end at death or return to work, and the punitive damages limits all directly cut the payouts insurers must make.

industries.industry: Hospitals, health plans, and managed care
industries.note: The definition of a 'health care liability action' covers any entity obligated to provide or pay for health benefits under a health plan, so HMOs and hospital systems get the same $250,000 cap and shortened filing window as individual doctors.

industries.industry: Corporate defendants generally (manufacturers and their insurers)
industries.note: The bill's findings argue that unlimited punitive damages and joint liability burden interstate commerce; the bill answers with a nationwide punitive damages standard, a one-award-per-conduct rule, and separate liability for noneconomic damages, all of which lower the cost of being sued.

A 'Trial Lawyer Accountability' section pushes states to make attorneys disclose hours and referral fees on contingency cases, the Attorney General is directed to draft model state legislation to curb contingency fees, mandatory Rule 11 sanctions replace discretionary ones, and plaintiffs who reject offers and win less at trial owe the defense's fees. Because these lawyers are paid only if injured clients recover, their interest in this bill ran alongside their clients'.

Requiring asset disclosure and ability-based filing fees, mandating dismissal of insubstantial claims, and forcing exhaustion of prison grievance systems before a civil rights suit all reduce inmate litigation against corrections agencies.
